title: "Policy Model"
sidebar-title: "Policy Model"
description: "The APF policy model from the author's perspective: control families, document kinds, decisions, rule ordering, defaults, and why APF uses Cedar."
keywords: "Generative AI, Cybersecurity, AI Agents, Policy Model, Cedar, PolicyRule, SandboxPolicy, Annotators, Effects, Findings, Policy Information Providers"
position: 1
---

APF policy is a set of YAML documents, each with one concern and usually one owning team. Together they express three things: what an agent can reach at all, which tools and actions it may use, and what content may flow through those actions. This page explains the model. The pages that follow cover each document kind.

## A First Example

This rule lets an agent post to Slack only in one approved channel and only short messages:

```yaml
apiVersion: nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1
kind: PolicyRule
metadata:
  name: slack-grants
spec:
  language: cedar
  role: capability
  data:
    approved_channel: "C0123456789"
    max_text_len: 500
  definition: |
    @id("slack-grants/slack_chat_post")
    permit (
      principal,
      action == APF::Action::"slack_chat_post",
      resource
    )
    when {
      context.args.channel == context.data.approved_channel &&
      context.args.text_len <= context.data.max_text_len
    };
```

The Cedar statement decides. `text_len` is derived by APF from the `text` argument's length. The demo bundle's copy of this rule reads `textLen` instead, which only a caller can supply. The `data` block holds the values an operator tunes, so changing the approved channel is a data change, not a logic change. The `role: capability` marks the rule as a grant for a tool. Any `role` other than exactly `control`, including a misspelling or `Control`, also makes the rule a grant, so validate rules against the [JSON Schemas](/reference/policy-schemas).

## Three Control Families

| Family | Question it answers | Documents | Where it is enforced |
|---|---|---|---|
| Containment | What can the sandbox attempt at all? Which hosts, files, and processes? | `SandboxPolicy` | OpenShell, from the projection, at Layer 1. |
| Capability | Which tools, methods, and resources may the agent use? | `SandboxPolicy` endpoint access and L7 rules, `Provider` profiles, and `PolicyRule` documents with `role: capability`. | OpenShell at Layer 1 for endpoints and methods. APF at Layer 2 for tool calls. |
| Content and context | Does this call, with these arguments and this body, hold up? | `PolicyAnnotator`, `PolicyRule` with `role: control`, `PolicyEffect`, `PolicyFinding`. | APF at Layer 2. |

## Document Kinds

| Kind | `apiVersion` | Concern | When it runs | Typical owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SandboxPolicy` | `nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.sandbox/v1alpha1` | Perimeter: network, filesystem, process, Landlock. | At sandbox admission, and again when a running sandbox is refreshed. | Platform or security. |
| `Provider` | `nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1` | Reachable services and their credentials. | Projected into OpenShell provider profiles. | Platform or tool owners. |
| `PolicyAnnotator` | `nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1` | Detection: derive signals from request content. | Stage 2, every request. | Security or compliance. |
| `PolicyRule` | `nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1` | Decision: permit or forbid, in Cedar. | Stage 3, every request. | Tool owners and platform. |
| `PolicyEffect` | `nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1` | Enforcement: rewrite the body, set headers, raise the verdict. | Stage 4, when a permit that references it fires. | Security or compliance. |
| `PolicyFinding` | `nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1` | Observability: a named audit signal. | Alongside any decision that references it. | Security or compliance. |

A bundle may also carry OpenShell-native provider profiles. Refer to [Sandbox Policies](/author-policies/sandbox-policies#providers).

Policy information providers are not documents. They are registered with the gateway, and their facts reach rules through the context in Stage 1. Refer to [Policy Information Providers](/integrations/policy-information-providers).

Every document shares the same envelope. `metadata.name` is required and identifies the document within its kind. `metadata.title`, `metadata.description`, and `metadata.version` are optional. The authoring schemas reject `metadata.namespace`.

```yaml
apiVersion: nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1
kind: <Kind>
metadata:
  name: <name>
spec:
  ...
```

## Principal, Action, Resource, and Context

Cedar evaluates each request as a principal performing an action on a resource, in a context.

| Slot | Populated from | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `principal` | The user subject the caller asserts, when it supplies one. | `APF::User::"alice@example.com"` |
| `action` | The tool, and the capability when the caller supplies one. | `APF::Action::"github_repo_read"` |
| `resource` | The tool being called. | `APF::Tool::"github_repo_read"` |
| `context` | Body, target, arguments, annotations, provider facts, and the rule's data. | `context.args.channel` |

On the OpenShell middleware path, the action and resource come from the MCP tool name, and the principal subject is empty. Refer to [Request Evaluation](/how-it-works/request-evaluation#cedar-request-mapping) for the exact mapping and every context attribute.

### Provider Context

Facts from policy information providers appear as `context.<domain>`, one record per registered domain. The record holds the provider's claims and a `_meta` record with `provider`, `verified`, `age_seconds`, `degraded`, `cached`, `status`, and `evidence_ref`. Policies name domains, not providers.

The roots `args`, `annotations`, `data`, `body_text`, `has_tool_name`, `target_host`, `target_method`, `target_path`, and `target_scheme` belong to the request and the engine. A domain can never use one of them.

```cedar
@id("change-grants/github_merge_pull_request")
permit (
  principal,
  action == APF::Action::"github_merge_pull_request",
  resource
)
when {
  context.change has approval &&
  context.change.approval == "approved"
};
```

Guard a permit with `has`. When the provider degraded or holds nothing for the request, the record carries only `_meta`, and the guard keeps the grant off. A forbid that reads a missing provider fact fails to evaluate and denies the request. Providers are registered with the gateway, not in the bundle. Refer to [Policy Information Providers](/integrations/policy-information-providers).

## Decisions

Every evaluation ends in one of three outcomes.

| Outcome | How it happens | What OpenShell does |
|---|---|---|
| Allow | No `forbid` fired, and, if the request is an MCP tool call, a capability grant permitted it. A request that is not a tool call needs no grant. | Forwards the request unchanged. |
| Allow with obligations | A `permit` that references `@apf_effect` or `@apf_finding` fired. | Applies the body and header changes, records the findings, then forwards the request. |
| Deny | A `forbid` fired, an MCP tool call received no grant, or evaluation failed on the OpenShell path. | Blocks the request. |

An allow can also carry an advisory verdict of `warn` or `escalate` from an effect. The verdict is recorded but does not block the request. No component acts on `escalate` with a review step yet.

## Ordering, Conflicts, and Defaults

- **Manifest order is semantic.** Rules are evaluated in the order the bundle manifest lists them. The first `forbid` that fires stops evaluation and determines the deny reason.
- **Default deny is a skip.** A rule in which no statement matches does not deny the request. Evaluation continues with the next rule.
- **Grants are required for tool calls.** An MCP tool call is denied unless at least one `capability` rule fires a `permit`. A `control` rule's permit does not count.
- **Plain HTTP requests are allowed by default.** A request that is not a tool call and that reaches APF is allowed unless a rule forbids it. Use the sandbox policy to keep the perimeter deny-by-default.
- **Effects aggregate deterministically.** Patches apply in firing order, but any body replacement discards them and the last replacement wins. Headers accumulate, and the strongest verdict wins.

## Evaluation Errors

APF fails closed at both load time and request time.

- **Load time.** A Cedar syntax error, a schema type error, an `@apf_effect` on a `forbid`, an unresolved effect or finding reference, an invalid annotator pattern, or a duplicate annotation name stops the evaluator from being built. The gateway refuses to start with that policy, or keeps its current evaluator when the bad policy arrives as an update.
- **Request time.** On the OpenShell path, an evaluation error, a missing annotation that an effect reads with `source`, or an effect that cannot be applied denies the request. `EvaluationService` returns an `INTERNAL` error for an evaluation error instead. A Cedar error inside a `permit`, such as reading a missing attribute, means that permit grants nothing. The same error inside a `forbid` denies the request, because a forbid that silently stops applying would turn a missing attribute into a grant. A policy information provider registered to fail closed that cannot answer denies the request with the reason `pip_<status>:<provider>` before any rule runs.

Refer to [Validate and Test Policies](/author-policies/validate-and-test-policies) to catch load-time errors before you sign.

## Why Cedar

APF uses [Cedar](https://www.cedarpolicy.com) as its decision language because governance policy must be auditable by the teams it affects, not only by the team that wrote it. Cedar trades expressiveness for auditability. Its deliberate constraints of no recursion, no side effects, and no I/O keep that guarantee as bundles grow.

- **Readable decisions.** A `permit` or `forbid` statement can be reviewed by security, legal, and compliance teams without policy-engineering expertise.
- **Static type checking.** When a rule supplies `spec.schema`, every policy in the rule is validated against it when the evaluator is built, so a misspelled field fails before any request is evaluated.
- **Analyzable policy sets.** Cedar's analysis tooling can reason about a policy set's coverage and conflicts. APF does not ship that tooling.
- **Safe composition.** Each `PolicyRule` is its own policy set with its own data, so one team's rule cannot change how another team's rule evaluates.

Cedar alone cannot express detection, such as regular expressions, length checks, or numeric coercion, or mutation, such as body redaction or header injection. APF adds an annotator stage before Cedar and an effect stage after it for those concerns. `spec.language` is the extension point for other languages. Cedar is the only language registered today, and any other value fails compilation.

## Next Steps

- To divide ownership across teams, refer to [Federated Authoring](/author-policies/federated-authoring).
- To write the perimeter, refer to [Sandbox Policies](/author-policies/sandbox-policies).
- To write tool grants, refer to [Capability Grants](/author-policies/capability-grants).

title: "Validate and Test Policies"
sidebar-title: "Validate and Test Policies"
description: "Catch policy errors before you sign: validate documents against the authoring schemas, verify bundles offline, build the evaluator locally, and exercise decisions."
keywords: "Generative AI, Cybersecurity, AI Agents, Policy Testing, Validation, JSON Schema, apf-compile, Cedar, grpcurl"
position: 8
---

A policy error found after signing costs a new revision. APF checks policy at several points, and each catches a different class of mistake. Run them in order before you sign and publish a bundle.

| Check | Catches | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| Schema validation | Unknown fields, wrong types, invalid enum values, invalid endpoint combinations, provider credential styles without their companion field, mistyped `kind` and `role` values. | Any JSON Schema 2020-12 validator with the schemas in `contracts/jsonschema/`. |
| Offline verification | Bad signatures, digest mismatches, an expired validity window. | `apf-compile compile --verify-only` |
| Offline compilation | Unparseable members, missing or duplicate document names, unknown `spec` fields, unsupported `language`, malformed `data`. A member with an unrecognized `kind` is skipped without an error. | `apf-compile compile` |
| Evaluator build | Cedar syntax and schema errors, misplaced or dangling `@apf_effect` and `@apf_finding`, invalid annotator patterns and operations, duplicate annotation keys. | A local `apf-policy-gateway` |
| Decision tests | Rules that compile but decide the wrong thing. | The gateway's `EvaluationService`, or a sandbox and `curl`. |

<Note>
The policy service verifies and compiles a bundle, but Cedar policies, annotators, and effects are compiled into an evaluator only by the policy gateway. A bundle with a Cedar syntax error loads into the policy service and is rejected by the gateway. Build the evaluator locally before you publish.
</Note>

## Validate Documents Against the Schemas

The repository ships JSON Schemas for every authored document kind:

| Schema | Documents |
|---|---|
| `policy-bundle.v1alpha1.schema.json` | The bundle manifest template. |
| `sandbox-policy.v1alpha1.schema.json` | `SandboxPolicy` |
| `provider.v1alpha1.schema.json` | `Provider` |
| `policy-rule.v1alpha1.schema.json` | `PolicyRule` |
| `policy-annotator.v1alpha1.schema.json` | `PolicyAnnotator` |
| `policy-effect.v1alpha1.schema.json` | `PolicyEffect` |
| `policy-finding.v1alpha1.schema.json` | `PolicyFinding` |

Validate each YAML document with a JSON Schema validator that accepts YAML input. For example, with the `check-jsonschema` CLI:

```shell
check-jsonschema \
  --schemafile contracts/jsonschema/policy-rule.v1alpha1.schema.json \
  bundle/rules/*.yaml
```

The bundle schema describes the manifest and requires each `sha256` to be 64 hexadecimal characters. A template still holds `REPLACE_WITH_DIGEST` placeholders, which the schema reports as invalid, so validate the member documents with their schemas and let the signer fill in the manifest digests.

## Verify and Compile Offline

`apf-compile compile` runs the same verification the policy service runs, against a trust-root directory you choose and a fresh, temporary anti-rollback counter:

```shell
./target/release/apf-compile compile \
  --bundle-path bundle/my-bundle.yaml \
  --trust-root-dir trust-roots \
  --verify-only
```

Drop `--verify-only` to also load and parse every member. The command prints the surfaces it produced. It does not register the OpenShell projector, so the sandbox policy projection is not included in its output.

Because the counter store is temporary, this command cannot tell you whether the revision is higher than the one a running policy service accepted. Refer to [Expiry and Rollback Protection](/manage-policy-bundles/expiry-and-rollback-protection).

## Build the Evaluator Locally

Run a local policy service and policy gateway on the bundle, as described in [Installation](/get-started/installation). Point `--bundle-path` and `--trust-root-dir` at your bundle and trust roots, and use a fresh `--counter-store`.

If any rule, annotator, effect, or finding fails to compile, the gateway refuses to start and names the problem, for example:

```text
Error: build initial Cedar evaluator

Caused by:
    build Cedar evaluator: evaluator engine error: rule 'slack-grants': policy parse: ...
```

Errors name the document, such as `rule '<name>'` or `annotator '<name>' annotation '<key>'`, so you can go straight to the file.

## Exercise Decisions

### With the Evaluation Service

The gateway's `EvaluationService` answers direct decision requests over its Unix socket. It is useful for testing capability grants. It maps `resource.class` to the tool and `verb` to the capability: the Cedar action is `APF::Action::"<class>::<verb>"`, or `APF::Action::"<class>"` when `verb` is empty, so an MCP tool name sent as the class exercises the same grant the OpenShell middleware evaluates for that tool call. `args` are passed as strings. The request carries no body or target, so content controls that read them are not exercised. A request without `resource` carries no tool: capability grants do not apply and the control rules decide, as for non-MCP traffic.

```shell
grpcurl -plaintext \
  -import-path contracts/proto \
  -proto nvidia/agent_policy_fabric/pdp/v1alpha1/pdp.proto \
  -d '{"resource": {"class": "github_repo_write", "id": "octo/repo"}}' \
  "unix://$SOCK_DIR/policy-gateway.sock" \
  nvidia.agent_policy_fabric.pdp.v1alpha1.EvaluationService/Evaluate
```

Pass the socket path as a `unix://` target. The `-unix` flag of grpcurl 1.9.3 has no effect.

Against the demo bundle, this request is denied: `github-grants` permits only `github_repo_read`, and nothing permits a write:

```text
{
  "decision": "DECISION_DENY",
  "policyDigestHex": "<digest>",
  "reason": "no grant for github_repo_write"
}
```

Send `github_repo_read` as the class instead and the decision is `DECISION_ALLOW`.

The caller must run as the UID the gateway's `--allowed-uid` allows, which defaults to the gateway's own UID.

### With a Sandbox

To exercise the full Layer 2 path, including annotators, content controls, and effects, send requests from inside a governed sandbox. APF identifies MCP tool calls from the JSON-RPC body, so you can test tool grants with a `tools/call` envelope sent to any host the sandbox policy routes to APF's middleware. Refer to [Your First Governed Agent](/get-started/your-first-governed-agent) for examples, and read the decisions in the middleware audit file.

### With Rust Tests

The evaluator is the `apf_policy_eval::CedarEvaluator` type, built from rule, annotator, effect, and finding documents. The repository's own tests in `crates/apf-policy-eval/src/cedar/` show how to construct an evaluator and assert on decisions, deny reasons, mutations, and findings.

## Next Steps

- To sign the validated bundle, refer to [Compile and Sign](/manage-policy-bundles/compile-and-sign).
- To understand each rejection, refer to [Error Reference](/reference/error-reference).

title: "Sandbox Policies and Providers"
sidebar-title: "Sandbox Policies"
description: "Author the SandboxPolicy that sets a sandbox's network, filesystem, and process perimeter, and the Provider documents that declare reachable services."
keywords: "Generative AI, Cybersecurity, AI Agents, SandboxPolicy, Network Policy, L7 Rules, Landlock, Provider, Containment"
position: 3
---

A `SandboxPolicy` sets the perimeter of every sandbox admitted under the bundle: which hosts it can reach and how, which paths it can read and write, and which identity its processes run as. APF projects it into OpenShell's sandbox policy when the bundle is loaded and injects it at admission, and OpenShell enforces it at Layer 1 on every call. APF does not evaluate it per request.

`Provider` documents declare the services an agent may use and the credentials OpenShell injects for them.

## A First Example

This policy lets `gh` and `curl` read from the GitHub API and nothing else:

```yaml
apiVersion: nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.sandbox/v1alpha1
kind: SandboxPolicy
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  filesystem:
    include_workdir: true
    read_only: [/usr, /lib, /etc]
    read_write: [/sandbox, /tmp]
  landlock:
    compatibility: best_effort
  process:
    run_as_user: sandbox
    run_as_group: sandbox
  network_policies:
    github:
      name: github
      binaries:
        - path: /usr/bin/gh
        - path: /usr/bin/curl
      endpoints:
        - host: api.github.com
          port: 443
          protocol: rest
          access: read-only
          enforcement: enforce
```

Egress is deny-by-default. Only the endpoints listed under `network_policies` are reachable, and only by the listed binaries.

## Which Sandbox Policy Is Used

The interceptor injects the `SandboxPolicy` whose `metadata.name` matches the gateway's `--document-name`, which defaults to `default`. A bundle may carry several sandbox policies with different names, and each projects to its own `openshell.sandbox.v1/<name>` document.

## Filesystem, Landlock, and Process

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `filesystem.include_workdir` | Adds the sandbox working directory as read-write. |
| `filesystem.read_only` | Paths the sandbox may read but not write. |
| `filesystem.read_write` | Paths the sandbox may read and write. |
| `landlock.compatibility` | How Landlock enforcement behaves on hosts with partial support. Use `best_effort`. The authoring schema also lists `required` and `disabled`, but OpenShell 0.1.x accepts only `best_effort` and `hard_requirement` and rejects other values at admission. |
| `process.run_as_user`, `process.run_as_group` | The identity the sandbox process runs as. |

These values pass through to OpenShell unchanged. Refer to [OpenShell sandbox policies](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/policies/overview) for how OpenShell enforces each one.

## Network Policies

`network_policies` is a map of named rules. Each rule lists endpoints and, optionally, the binaries allowed to open connections to them. The map key identifies the rule. `name` defaults to the key.

### Endpoints

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `host` | Host name or host glob. |
| `port` or `ports` | One port, or a list of ports. One of the two is required. |
| `path` | HTTP path glob that scopes the endpoint on a shared host and port. |
| `protocol` | `tcp`, `rest`, `websocket`, `graphql`, `sql`, `json-rpc`, or `mcp`. Omit it for Layer 4 only. |
| `tls` | Omit it to keep OpenShell's automatic TLS termination, or set `skip` to turn TLS inspection off. The authoring schema lists `terminate` and `passthrough`, which OpenShell 0.1.x rejects, and does not list `skip`. OpenShell also refuses a fail-closed middleware entry, such as APF's, that selects a `skip` host. |
| `enforcement` | `enforce` blocks violations. `audit` logs them without blocking. When omitted, OpenShell audits. OpenShell rejects `enforce` for `sql` endpoints. |
| `access` | A preset: `read-only`, `read-write`, or `full`. |
| `rules` | Explicit Layer 7 allow rules. Mutually exclusive with `access`. |
| `deny_rules` | Explicit Layer 7 deny rules, evaluated after allow rules. |
| `allowed_ips` | IP addresses or CIDR ranges the host may resolve to. |
| `mcp` | MCP options: `strict_tool_names` and `allow_all_known_mcp_methods`. `max_body_bytes` is used as `json_rpc_max_body_bytes` when that field is not set. |

The authoring schema enforces these combinations:

- `tcp` endpoints cannot use `access`, `rules`, `deny_rules`, or `enforcement`.
- `rest`, `websocket`, `graphql`, and `sql` endpoints need `access` or at least one rule.
- `json-rpc` endpoints need at least one rule and cannot use `access`.
- `mcp` endpoints need at least one rule or `mcp.allow_all_known_mcp_methods: true`, and cannot use `access`.
- `deny_rules` require a Layer 7 protocol.

### Layer 7 Rules

Each entry in `rules` has one `allow` object. Each entry in `deny_rules` is the match object itself. The fields that apply depend on the protocol:

| Field | Protocols |
|---|---|
| `method`, `path`, `query` | `rest`, and `method` for `json-rpc` and `mcp` |
| `command` | `sql` |
| `operation_type`, `operation_name`, `fields` | `graphql` |
| `params` | `mcp`, where only `params.name` is supported for `tools/call` filtering |

```yaml
endpoints:
  - host: httpbin.org
    port: 443
    protocol: rest
    enforcement: enforce
    rules:
      - allow:
          method: POST
          path: /anything
```

Refer to [OpenShell network rules](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/policies/network-rules) for the matching semantics of each protocol and preset.

### Binaries

`binaries` restricts which executables may open connections governed by the rule. Each entry has a `path`. Refer to [OpenShell network rules](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/policies/network-rules) for how OpenShell identifies the calling binary.

### Credential Controls

Endpoints can also carry `request_body_credential_rewrite` and `websocket_credential_rewrite`. APF accepts `credential_binding` and `allow_uninspected_credentials` but does not project them in this release: OpenShell always receives no binding and `allow_uninspected_credentials: false`. Refer to [Credential Integration](/how-it-works/credential-integration#binding-credentials-to-endpoints).

## Selecting APF's Middleware

`network_middlewares` attaches supervisor middleware to destination hosts. Add an entry that selects APF's middleware for every host whose requests APF should evaluate at Layer 2:

```yaml
network_middlewares:
  apf_content_policy:
    name: APF content policy
    middleware: apf-content-policy
    order: 10
    on_error: fail_closed
    endpoints:
      include:
        - "api.github.com"
        - "httpbin.org"
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `middleware` | The OpenShell registration name of APF's middleware. |
| `order` | Run order relative to other middleware on the same host. Lower runs first. |
| `on_error` | `fail_closed` blocks traffic when the middleware fails. `fail_open` lets it through. Use `fail_closed` for APF. |
| `endpoints.include`, `endpoints.exclude` | Host selectors. OpenShell allows at most 32 patterns across both lists. |

APF's middleware takes no configuration, so an APF `SandboxPolicy` has no `config` field for it, and a `config` key fails compilation. The authoring schema allows at most 10 middleware entries, and OpenShell requires each entry's `order` to be unique. APF does not check either limit. A host that no entry selects is never evaluated by APF, even if it is reachable at Layer 1.

## Providers

A `Provider` document declares a service the agent may use: its category, endpoints, permitted binaries, and credentials.

```yaml
apiVersion: nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1
kind: Provider
metadata:
  name: slack
  title: Slack
  description: Slack Web API, workspace messaging.
spec:
  type: messaging
  endpoints:
    - host: slack.com
      port: 443
      protocol: rest
      access: read-write
      enforcement: enforce
  binaries:
    - /usr/bin/curl
  credentials:
    - name: bot_token
      envVars: [SLACK_TOKEN]
      required: true
      style: bearer
      header: Authorization
      source:
        kind: host-env
        name: SLACK_TOKEN
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `spec.type` | Provider category: `inference`, `agent`, `source-control`, `messaging`, `data`, or `knowledge`. Any other value projects as `other`. |
| `spec.endpoints` | The destinations this provider's credentials may reach. Each needs a host and a port. Same fields as sandbox endpoints. |
| `spec.binaries` | Executables permitted to use this provider. Each entry is a path string or an object with `path`. |
| `spec.credentials` | Credentials the provider uses. Refer to [Credential Integration](/how-it-works/credential-integration). |

Bundles may also carry OpenShell-native provider profiles as `kind: ProviderProfile` documents or as profiles with a top-level `id` and `endpoints`. They pass through unchanged. When a `Provider` and a native profile share a name, the `Provider` wins.

When APF governs the OpenShell gateway, providers and profiles that the bundle does not manage cannot be created or imported. Refer to [Credential Integration](/how-it-works/credential-integration#governing-providers-at-the-gateway).

- For the full field list, refer to [Policy Schemas](/reference/policy-schemas#sandboxpolicy).

keywords: "Generative AI, Cybersecurity, AI Agents, Authentication, mTLS, TLS, JWT, Extension Auth, Trust Profile, Bearer Token, Unix Socket"

An APF deployment has several connections, and each is authenticated differently. This page covers each one and how to configure it.

| Connection | Authenticated by | Configured with |
|---|---|---|
| OpenShell gateway to the APF interceptor | OpenShell extension JWT over TLS | Interceptor trust profile, certificate, and key |
| Sandbox supervisor to the APF middleware | OpenShell extension JWT over TLS, bound to the sandbox | Middleware trust profile, certificate, and key |
| Policy gateway to policy service | Unix socket permissions and peer UID | `--allowed-uid` |
| Policy gateway to the policy service JWKS endpoint | None. The route is public, and the keys it serves are public keys. Bind the HTTP surface to loopback. | `--jwks-url` on the gateway, `--http-addr` on the policy service |
| Co-located caller to the gateway's `EvaluationService` | Unix socket permissions and peer UID | `--allowed-uid` on the gateway |
| Policy gateway to the OpenShell gateway, for provider reconciliation and sandbox refresh | None. The connection uses no TLS and no credentials. | `--openshell-gateway-url` |
| Anyone to the policy service HTTP surface | Bearer token on document and refresh routes | `--http-bearer-token-file` |
| Policy service to an HTTP bundle source | Bearer token | `--bundle-source-token-file` |

## OpenShell Extension Authentication

When OpenShell's gateway has JWT signing configured, it attaches a short-lived extension JWT to every call into an interceptor or middleware. APF verifies that token against a static trust profile, one per listener. The trust profile is a separate trust domain from APF's bundle trust roots and from the policy service's JWKS. Never substitute one for another.

### The Trust Profile

The trust profile is strict TOML. Unknown fields are rejected.

```toml
issuer = "openshell-gateway:<gateway-id>"
audience = "urn:openshell:extension:middleware:apf-content-policy"
kid = "<OpenShell signing key ID>"
public_key_pem = """
-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
<OpenShell Ed25519 public key>
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----
"""
max_lifetime_secs = 3600
leeway_secs = 60
```

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `issuer` | The OpenShell gateway's identity, `openshell-gateway:<gateway-id>`. |
| `audience` | The audience in the OpenShell registration. If the registration omits `audience`, OpenShell uses `urn:openshell:extension:interceptor:<registration name>` for an interceptor and `urn:openshell:extension:middleware:<registration name>` for a middleware. Copy the exact value. |
| `kid` | The key ID of OpenShell's extension signing key. |
| `public_key_pem` | OpenShell's Ed25519 public key in PEM form. |
| `max_lifetime_secs` | The longest token lifetime APF accepts, from 1 to 3600. |
| `leeway_secs` | Allowed clock skew, at most 300. |

Obtain the issuer, key ID, and public key from your OpenShell gateway's configuration. Refer to [OpenShell extension authentication](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/extensibility/overview#authenticating-extensions). On Kubernetes, the OpenShell chart's pre-install Job writes the key ID and public key to the `<fullname>-jwt-keys` Secret as `kid` and `public.pem`; refer to [Trust Profiles](/deployment/kubernetes#trust-profiles).

APF accepts exactly one `authorization: Bearer <JWT>` value and requires `alg` `EdDSA`, `typ` `openshell-ext+jwt`, the configured `kid`, the exact issuer and audience, a non-empty `jti`, and a bounded, unexpired lifetime.

### Caller Rules

| Surface | RPC | Accepted caller |
|---|---|---|
| Interceptor | `Describe`, `SnapshotProviderProfiles`, `Evaluate` | The OpenShell gateway only. |
| Middleware | `Describe` | The OpenShell gateway or a sandbox supervisor. |
| Middleware | `ValidateConfig` | The OpenShell gateway only. |
| Middleware | `EvaluateHttpRequest` | A sandbox supervisor only, and the token's `sandbox_id` must equal the request's sandbox ID. |

A gateway token's subject equals its issuer and carries no `sandbox_id`. A supervisor token's subject is `spiffe://openshell/sandbox/<sandbox-id>` and carries a matching `sandbox_id` claim.

### TLS Identity

Each authenticated listener also presents a TLS certificate. The certificate must be valid for the host name in the OpenShell registration's `grpc_endpoint` and must chain to a CA that OpenShell trusts. Give OpenShell that CA with `tls_ca_cert_path` in the registration.

### Configure a Listener

Set all four settings for a surface together. The gateway refuses to start a surface with a partial set, and refuses security files for a surface whose address is not set.

```shell
apf-policy-gateway \
  --openshell-interceptor-addr 127.0.0.1:18202 \
  --openshell-interceptor-auth-trust-file /etc/apf/openshell-interceptor-auth.toml \
  --openshell-interceptor-tls-cert-file /etc/apf/tls/interceptor-cert.pem \
  --openshell-interceptor-tls-key-file /etc/apf/tls/interceptor-key.pem \
  --openshell-middleware-addr 127.0.0.1:9099 \
  --openshell-middleware-auth-trust-file /etc/apf/openshell-middleware-auth.toml \
  --openshell-middleware-tls-cert-file /etc/apf/tls/middleware-cert.pem \
  --openshell-middleware-tls-key-file /etc/apf/tls/middleware-key.pem \
  --jwks-url http://127.0.0.1:19200/.well-known/jwks.json \
  --audit-log-dir /var/lib/apf/policy-gateway/audit
```

The interceptor needs `--jwks-url` to verify provenance tokens, and the gateway refuses to start the interceptor without it.

Each flag has an environment variable equivalent, for example `APF_OPENSHELL_MIDDLEWARE_AUTH_TRUST_FILE`. Refer to [CLI Commands](/reference/cli-commands#apf-policy-gateway).

### File Checks

The gateway opens each security file without following a symbolic link and checks the opened file:

- The trust profile and certificate must be regular files with no group or world write permission.
- The private key must be a regular file with no group or world permission at all, normally mode `0600` or `0400`.
- Directories, FIFOs, sockets, devices, and symbolic links are rejected.

The gateway parses all three files into its TLS configuration before any listener reports ready. Any failure stops the process instead of falling back to plaintext.

### Insecure Mode

`--openshell-interceptor-allow-insecure-transport` and `--openshell-middleware-allow-insecure-transport` turn off TLS and caller authentication for one surface. The surface serves plaintext gRPC, verifies no caller, performs no sandbox binding, advertises an empty audience, and logs a warning at startup. The insecure flag cannot be combined with any authenticated setting for the same surface. Pair it with `allow_insecure_transport = true` in the OpenShell registration, and use it only for local development.

## Unix Socket Access

The policy service socket and the gateway's `EvaluationService` socket are created with mode `0600` in a directory with mode `0700`. Each service also reads the connecting peer's UID with `SO_PEERCRED` and accepts only the UID set by `--allowed-uid`, `APF_ALLOWED_UID` for the policy service and `APF_GATEWAY_ALLOWED_UID` for the gateway. Both default to the service's own UID.

The policy service records each refused peer as an `authentication` event with `auth.uds_peer_rejected`, and reports refusals it could not record individually with `auth.uds_refusals_dropped`.

## Policy Service HTTP Token

With `--http-addr` set, the policy service requires `--http-bearer-token-file` and refuses to start without it. The token gates `/v1/documents` and `/v1/refresh`. Health routes and the JWKS route stay open. Store the token as `root:root` with mode `0600` and deliver it as a systemd credential. A wrong token returns `401` and writes an `authentication` event with `auth.http_bearer_invalid`.

## Bundle Source Token

With the HTTP policy source, put the artifact store token in a file and pass `--bundle-source-token-file`. An empty file is an error. `--bundle-source-token` also works, but the token is then visible in the process arguments, and the startup record reports the weakened control.

## Next Steps

- To deploy these files on a host, refer to [Host and Workstation Deployment](/deployment/host-and-workstation-deployment).
- To see where each boundary sits, refer to [Trust Boundaries](/security/trust-boundaries).

title: "Annotators"
sidebar-title: "Annotators"
description: "Write PolicyAnnotator documents that detect and classify request content with regular expressions, comparisons, and length checks, and expose the results to Cedar."
keywords: "Generative AI, Cybersecurity, AI Agents, Annotators, Detection, Regex, Secrets, PII, Cedar Context"
position: 6
---

Annotators handle the detection logic Cedar cannot express: regular expressions, substring and suffix checks, numeric comparisons, and lengths. Each `PolicyAnnotator` derives named values from the raw request before any rule runs. Rules read the values as `context.annotations.<name>`, and effects can copy them into headers or finding labels.

## A First Example

This annotator flags credential-shaped text and labels its kind:

```yaml
apiVersion: nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1
kind: PolicyAnnotator
metadata:
  name: secret-detector
spec:
  description: Detects known credential shapes in request body text.
  annotations:
    - name: secret_detected
      output: bool
      set_true_if: any
      rules:
        - field: body_text
          op: regex_match
          pattern: 'ghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}'
        - field: body_text
          op: regex_match
          pattern: 'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}'

    - name: secret_kind
      output: string
      set_value_from: first_match
      rules:
        - field: body_text
          op: regex_match
          pattern: 'ghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{36}'
          value: github_pat
        - field: body_text
          op: regex_match
          pattern: 'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}'
          value: aws_access_key
```

A rule can now write `when { context.annotations.secret_detected }`, and an effect can set a header from `context.annotations.secret_kind`.

## Annotation Outputs

| `output` | Combinator | Present in context | Valid operations |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bool` | `set_true_if: any` (default) or `all` | Always. `false` when the rules do not match. | Predicate operations. |
| `string` | `set_value_from: first_match` | Only when a rule matched. The value is that rule's `value`. | Predicate operations. Every rule must set `value`. |
| `integer` | First rule that produces a value | Only when a rule produced a value. | `length` and `passthrough` only. |

Guard every string and integer annotation with `has` before you read it in Cedar:

```cedar
when {
  context.annotations has secret_kind &&
  context.annotations.secret_kind == "github_pat"
}
```

## Fields

Each rule reads one field of the request.

| `field` | Reads |
|---|---|
| `body_text` | The request body as text. For an MCP call this is the whole JSON-RPC envelope, including the arguments. |
| `body_json` | The whole parsed JSON body. |
| `body_json.<path>` | A value inside the JSON body. Use a dotted path such as `body_json.params.name`, or an RFC 6901 pointer such as `body_json./params/name`. |
| `args.<name>` | An MCP tool argument. |
| `target.host`, `target.path`, `target.method` | The request target. |
| `user_subject` | The user subject the caller asserts. Empty on the OpenShell middleware path. |

A field that does not exist in the request never matches.

## Operations

| `op` | Operand | Matches when |
|---|---|---|
| `regex_match` | `pattern` | The field is a string that matches the regular expression. |
| `equals` | `value` | The field is a string equal to `value`. |
| `startswith` | `prefix` | The field is a string that starts with `prefix`. |
| `endswith` | `suffix` | The field is a string that ends with `suffix`. |
| `contains` | `substring` | The field is a string that contains `substring`. |
| `gte` | `threshold` | The field is an integer, or a string that parses as one, greater than or equal to `threshold`. |
| `lte` | `threshold` | Same, less than or equal to `threshold`. |
| `length` | none | Integer output only. Produces the string's length in characters. |
| `passthrough` | none | Integer output only. Produces the field's integer value. |

Patterns use the syntax of the Rust `regex` crate, which is similar to RE2. Lookaround and backreferences are not supported.

## Producing Integers

Use an `integer` annotation to expose a number to Cedar, for example the length of a message:

```yaml
- name: message_length
  output: integer
  rules:
    - field: body_json.text
      op: length
```

```cedar
forbid (principal, action, resource)
when {
  context.annotations has message_length &&
  context.annotations.message_length > 4000
};
```

## Load-Time Checks

The evaluator rejects an annotator, and with it the whole policy, when:

- An annotation has no rules.
- A rule is missing its operation's operand, or its pattern does not compile.
- An operation does not fit the output type, such as `length` on a `bool` annotation.
- A `string` annotation's rule has no `value`.
- A field selector is not one of the supported forms.
- Two annotations anywhere in the bundle share a name.

## Writing Good Detectors

- Keep detection and decision separate. An annotator should say what it saw, and a rule should decide what to do about it.
- Use a `bool` annotation with `set_true_if: any` for a detection flag, and a `string` annotation with `set_value_from: first_match` for its classification. List the same patterns in both, in the same order.
- Every annotation runs on every request APF evaluates. Keep patterns specific.
- The repository's demo bundle includes `annotators/secret-detector.yaml` and `annotators/pii-detector.yaml` as starting points.

## Next Steps

- To act on these signals, refer to [Content Controls](/author-policies/content-controls).
- To copy annotation values into headers and findings, refer to [Effects and Findings](/author-policies/effects-and-findings).

title: "Content Controls"
sidebar-title: "Content Controls"
description: "Write control rules that inspect the content and context of every request, deny what must not leave the sandbox, and redact what may leave only in a safer form."
keywords: "Generative AI, Cybersecurity, AI Agents, Content Controls, Data Loss Prevention, Redaction, Cedar, Control Rules, Secrets, PII"
position: 5
---

Content controls decide whether an already-permitted call holds up given what it carries. They are `PolicyRule` documents with `role: control`. Control rules apply to all traffic that reaches APF, MCP tool calls and plain HTTP requests alike. Their permits never grant a tool call. Their forbids deny any request they match.

## A First Example

The demo bundle's `security-content-gate` denies MCP tool calls that carry a secret, and replaces the body of plain HTTP requests that carry one:

```yaml
apiVersion: nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1
kind: PolicyRule
metadata:
  name: security-content-gate
spec:
  description: Deny secret leakage, redact PII.
  language: cedar
  role: control
  definition: |
    @id("baseline-allow")
    permit (principal, action, resource);

    @apf_finding("secret-detected")
    @id("deny-secret")
    forbid (principal, action, resource)
    when { context.has_tool_name && context.annotations.secret_detected };

    @apf_effect("redact-wholesale")
    @id("redact-secret-rest")
    permit (principal, action, resource)
    when { !context.has_tool_name && context.annotations.secret_detected };

    @apf_effect("redact-pii-body")
    @id("redact-pii-rest")
    permit (principal, action, resource)
    when { !context.has_tool_name && context.annotations.pii_detected };
```

The rule reads two signals produced by annotators, `secret_detected` and `pii_detected`. Annotators do the inspection, Cedar decides, and effects carry out the rewrite.

## How a Control Rule Works

| Statement | Fires when | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `forbid` with `@apf_finding` | The condition matches. | The request is denied with reason `security-content-gate/deny-secret`, and the finding is recorded. Evaluation stops. |
| `permit` with `@apf_effect` | The condition matches. | The request continues, and the effect is applied if the request is finally allowed. |
| `permit` without annotations | The condition matches. | Nothing. A control permit does not grant a tool call. |

## Building Blocks

### Detection Signals

Read annotations with `context.annotations.<name>`. Bool annotations are always present. Guard string and integer annotations with `has`:

```cedar
forbid (principal, action, resource)
when {
  context.annotations has secret_kind &&
  context.annotations.secret_kind == "aws_access_key"
};
```

Refer to [Annotators](/author-policies/annotators).

### Traffic Type

`context.has_tool_name` is `true` for MCP tool calls and `false` for plain HTTP requests. Use it to treat the two differently in one rule, as the demo does.

### Request Target

`context.target_host`, `context.target_method`, `context.target_path`, and `context.target_scheme` describe the destination. They are present when the request has a target, which is always the case on the OpenShell middleware path.

```cedar
@id("block-uploads")
forbid (principal, action, resource)
when {
  context has target_method &&
  context.target_method == "PUT" &&
  !context.has_tool_name
};
```

### Tool Arguments

`context.args` carries MCP tool arguments, with `_len` and `_num` fields derived for string arguments. Refer to [Capability Grants](/author-policies/capability-grants#constraining-arguments).

## Choosing a Response

| Goal | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Block the request | `forbid`, optionally with `@apf_finding` to record why. |
| Let the request through in a safer form | `permit` with `@apf_effect` referencing a body replacement or patch. |
| Let the request through and flag it | `permit` with `@apf_effect` referencing an effect whose `verdict` is `warn` or `escalate`, or with `@apf_finding` alone. |
| Record an observation only | `permit` with `@apf_finding`. The decision is unchanged and the finding is recorded. |

## Fail-Closed Rewrites

A rewrite that cannot be applied denies the request, because forwarding the original would drop a mandated change.

- A body patch requires a JSON body. A patch on a non-JSON body denies the request.
- A `replace` or `remove` patch on a path the body does not contain denies the request. The demo's `redact-pii-body` effect replaces `/text`, so a plain HTTP request that contains PII but has no top-level `text` field is denied.
- An effect that reads an annotation with `source` denies the request if that annotation was not produced.

Prefer a whole-body replacement when you cannot predict the body's shape.

## Scope

Content controls see the request only. APF binds the supervisor middleware's request operation, so it does not inspect responses or WebSocket messages, and it never sees credentials, which OpenShell injects after APF decides. Refer to [Enforcement Coverage and Limitations](/security/enforcement-coverage-and-limitations).

## Next Steps

- To write the detectors these rules read, refer to [Annotators](/author-policies/annotators).
- To define rewrites and findings, refer to [Effects and Findings](/author-policies/effects-and-findings).
- To try these controls end to end, refer to [Protect Sensitive Data](/tutorials/protect-sensitive-data).

title: "Capability Grants"
sidebar-title: "Capability Grants"
description: "Write PolicyRule documents with role capability that grant agents specific tool calls, constrain their arguments, and keep tunable values in data blocks."
keywords: "Generative AI, Cybersecurity, AI Agents, Capability Grants, Cedar, PolicyRule, MCP Tools, Least Privilege, Policy Information Providers"
position: 4
---

A capability grant says which tool calls an agent may make and under which argument constraints. Grants are `PolicyRule` documents with `role: capability`. Every MCP tool call that reaches APF must be permitted by at least one grant, so a tool without a grant is denied by default.

## A First Example

This rule permits only the `github_repo_read` tool. There is no permit for a write tool, so an MCP call to one is denied:

```yaml
apiVersion: nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1
kind: PolicyRule
metadata:
  name: github-grants
spec:
  description: Grants for GitHub tool capabilities. repo_write has no permit.
  language: cedar
  role: capability
  definition: |
    @id("github-grants/repo_read")
    permit (
      principal,
      action == APF::Action::"github_repo_read",
      resource
    );
```

## Naming the Action

A grant matches the Cedar action APF builds for the request.

| Caller | Action |
|---|---|
| OpenShell supervisor middleware, for an MCP `tools/call` | `APF::Action::"<params.name>"`, for example `APF::Action::"github_repo_read"`. |
| `EvaluationService.Evaluate` with a `verb` | `APF::Action::"<resource.class>::<verb>"`, for example `APF::Action::"outlook::message_search"`. |
| `EvaluationService.Evaluate` with an empty `verb` | `APF::Action::"<resource.class>"`. Send the MCP tool name as the class to exercise a middleware grant, for example `APF::Action::"github_repo_read"`. |

The resource is `APF::Tool::"<tool>"`, where the tool is the MCP tool name on the middleware path and `resource.class` on the `Evaluate` path. Write grants for the path your callers use.

## Constraining Arguments

Tool arguments are available as `context.args.<name>`. For each string argument, APF also adds two derived fields, because Cedar has no string-length or numeric-coercion functions:

- `context.args.<name>_len`: the length of the string in characters.
- `context.args.<name>_num`: the string's integer value, present only when it parses as an integer.

```cedar
@id("outlook-grants/message_search")
permit (
  principal,
  action == APF::Action::"outlook_message_search",
  resource
)
when {
  context.args.folder == "inbox" &&
  context.args has limit_num &&
  context.args.limit_num <= 25
};
```

Guard any attribute that may be absent with `has`. Reading a missing attribute is a Cedar evaluation error. A permit that errors grants nothing. A forbid that errors denies the request with the reason `<rule>/<@id>: evaluation error: <detail>`, so an unguarded forbid fails closed rather than silently stopping to protect you; guard it with `has` when it should not apply to requests that lack the attribute.

## Keeping Tunable Values in Data

Put operator-tunable values, such as an approved channel or a size limit, in `spec.data`. Each rule sees only its own data as `context.data`, so a tool owner can change a value without editing Cedar:

```yaml
spec:
  language: cedar
  role: capability
  data:
    approved_channel: "C0123456789"
    max_text_len: 500
  definition: |
    @id("slack-grants/slack_chat_post")
    permit (
      principal,
      action == APF::Action::"slack_chat_post",
      resource
    )
    when {
      context.args.channel == context.data.approved_channel &&
      context.args.text_len <= context.data.max_text_len
    };
```

`spec.data` must be a mapping. It does not influence the decision except through the conditions that read it.

## Grants That Depend on Provider Facts

A grant can read facts that a policy information provider supplied in the Enrichment stage, such as a change request's approval state, as `context.<domain>.<claim>`. Guard the read with `has`:

```cedar
@id("change-grants/github_merge_pull_request")
permit (
  principal,
  action == APF::Action::"github_merge_pull_request",
  resource
)
when {
  context.change has approval &&
  context.change.approval == "approved"
};
```

What happens when the provider cannot answer depends on its registration. With `on_failure: degrade`, `context.change` holds only its `_meta` record, with `degraded` set to `true`, so the guard keeps the grant off and the call is denied with `no grant for <action>`. With `on_failure: fail_closed`, the request is denied before any rule runs, with the reason `pip_<status>:<provider>`. The provider looks the change up by the repository the tool acts on, so the agent cannot choose which record gates its request. Refer to [Policy Information Providers](/integrations/policy-information-providers).

## Type-Checking with a Schema

Add a Cedar schema in `spec.schema` to catch misspelled fields and type errors when the evaluator is built, before any request runs. When a schema is present, every policy in the rule is validated against it, so the schema must declare each context attribute the policies read.

```yaml
spec:
  language: cedar
  role: capability
  schema: |
    namespace APF {
      entity User;
      entity Tool;
      action "slack_chat_post" appliesTo {
        principal: [User],
        resource: [Tool],
        context: {
          args: {
            channel: String,
            text_len: Long,
          },
          data: {
            approved_channel: String,
            max_text_len: Long,
          },
        }
      };
    }
  data:
    approved_channel: "C0123456789"
    max_text_len: 500
  definition: |
    @id("slack-grants/slack_chat_post")
    permit (principal, action == APF::Action::"slack_chat_post", resource)
    when {
      context.args.channel == context.data.approved_channel &&
      context.args.text_len <= context.data.max_text_len
    };
```

Do not put the schema at the top of `definition`. APF rejects a definition that starts with a schema declaration and asks you to move it into `spec.schema`.

## How Grants Combine

- Grants are evaluated in manifest order with the other rules. A grant whose statements do not match is skipped.
- One permit from any capability rule satisfies the grant requirement for a tool call.
- A `forbid` in any rule, including a capability rule, stops evaluation and denies the request.
- Grants are written against tool actions, so they normally match only tool calls. A request that is not a tool call needs no grant.

## Deny Reasons

When a tool call gets no grant, APF returns one of two reasons:

| Reason | When |
|---|---|
| `<rule>: conditions not met for <action>` | A capability rule whose name contains the full tool name was skipped. For OpenShell traffic the tool name is the whole MCP tool name, so a rule named `github-grants` does not match `github_repo_write`. |
| `no grant for <action>` | No capability rule's name contains the full tool name. |

An explicit `forbid` returns `<rule>/<@id>` instead, or the `@id` itself when it contains `/`, or `<rule>/policyN` when the statement has no `@id`. Use `@id("<rule>/<label>")` on every statement so deny reasons read clearly in audit records.

## Authoring Checklist

1. Use `role: capability` for tool grants and `role: control` for content policy. Any value other than exactly `control`, including a misspelling or `Control`, is treated as a grant.
2. Name grant rules after the tools they cover. A rule name that contains the full tool name gets the more specific deny reason.
3. Put tunable values in `spec.data`.
4. Add `spec.schema` for any rule that reads `context.args`.
5. Guard optional attributes and provider facts with `has`.
6. Give every statement an `@id`.

## Next Steps

- To inspect and rewrite content on allowed calls, refer to [Content Controls](/author-policies/content-controls).
- To exercise grants without a live agent, refer to [Validate and Test Policies](/author-policies/validate-and-test-policies).

title: "Federated Authoring"
sidebar-title: "Federated Authoring"
description: "How security, compliance, tool-owner, and platform teams contribute independent policy documents to one signed bundle, share detectors and effects, and review changes."
keywords: "Generative AI, Cybersecurity, AI Agents, Federated Authoring, Policy as Code, GitOps, Review, Ownership"
position: 2
---

Federated authoring lets each team own the policy in its domain without editing a shared codebase or coordinating every change. Security writes detectors and content gates, compliance writes data-handling controls, tool owners write grants for their tools, and the platform team writes the sandbox perimeter. All of it is signed into one bundle and enforced together.

## How Teams Divide the Work

Each document kind maps to a concern, so ownership follows the kind.

| Team | Typical documents |
|---|---|
| Platform | `SandboxPolicy` perimeter, `Provider` documents for shared services. |
| Security | `PolicyAnnotator` detectors such as `secret-detector`, `PolicyRule` documents with `role: control` such as `security-content-gate`, and the `PolicyFinding` and `PolicyEffect` documents they reference. |
| Compliance | Annotators and effects for regulated data, such as `pii-detector` and `redact-pii-body`. |
| Tool owners | `PolicyRule` documents with `role: capability` for their tools, such as `github-grants` or `slack-grants`, with operator-tunable values in `spec.data`. |

## Shared Components

Annotators, effects, and findings are shared infrastructure. They are written once and referenced by name from any rule in the bundle.

- Every annotation is available to every rule as `context.annotations.<name>`. The security team's `secret-detector` is visible to a tool owner's grant rule with no coordination.
- Any rule can reference an effect with `@apf_effect("<name>")` and a finding with `@apf_finding("<name>")`.
- A reference to an effect or finding that does not exist in the bundle is a load-time error, so a team cannot silently depend on a document that was removed.

Document names must be unique within each kind, and annotation names must be unique across all annotators. A duplicate is a load-time error. For a duplicate annotation name, the error names both annotators.

## A Policy Repository Layout

APF does not require a particular repository structure. A conventional layout keeps each bundle in its own directory, with one subdirectory per document kind:

```text
policy-repo/
  bundles/
    <bundle-name>/
      <bundle-name>.template.yaml
      sandbox/
      provider-profiles/
      annotators/
      findings/
      effects/
      rules/
```

Each bundle directory compiles and signs independently. Teams contribute to the bundles they are responsible for, and every change goes through pull request review before it is signed.

## Who Owns the Manifest

The manifest template lists every member and fixes their order. Rule order is semantic: the first `forbid` that fires decides the deny reason. Order also controls which effects run first and which annotator a duplicate-name error blames. Treat a reorder of the manifest as a policy change and review it as one.

The recommended manifest order is:

1. `SandboxPolicy` and provider documents.
2. `PolicyAnnotator` documents.
3. `PolicyFinding` and `PolicyEffect` documents.
4. `PolicyRule` documents, with the rules whose `forbid` reasons you want reported first listed first.

## Reviewing Changes

Every policy change is a document diff. Because each kind has one concern, a reviewer can read a change in isolation:

- An annotator change alters what is detected, not what is decided.
- A rule change alters what is decided.
- An effect change alters what is done to an allowed request.
- A `data` change alters a tunable value without touching logic.

An example of independent contributions to one bundle:

```text
Security team
  annotators/prompt-injection-detector.yaml   detects adversarial prompt patterns
  rules/security-content-gate.yaml            forbids on detection
  findings/prompt-injection.yaml

Agent owner
  rules/github-grants.yaml                    capability grants for the agent's tools
  effects/redact-code-secrets.yaml            redacts secrets before they leave the sandbox

Platform team
  sandbox/default-policy.yaml                 network perimeter for all sandboxes
```

After review and merge, the bundle is signed with a higher `policy_revision` and published. Refer to [Compile and Sign](/manage-policy-bundles/compile-and-sign).

APF does not provide a review or approval workflow of its own. Use your source control's review, branch protection, and code ownership features. A human-review gate inside APF is reserved in the audit schema but not implemented.

## Next Steps

- To check documents before review, refer to [Validate and Test Policies](/author-policies/validate-and-test-policies).
- To learn each document kind, continue with [Sandbox Policies](/author-policies/sandbox-policies).

title: "Effects and Findings"
sidebar-title: "Effects and Findings"
description: "Write PolicyEffect documents that rewrite allowed requests and raise verdicts, and PolicyFinding documents that record what policy observed."
keywords: "Generative AI, Cybersecurity, AI Agents, Effects, Findings, Redaction, JSON Patch, Headers, Verdict, Audit"
position: 7
---

Effects say what happens to a request that policy allows. Findings say what policy observed, whether the request was allowed or denied. Both are named documents that any rule in the bundle can reference.

| Document | Referenced with | Valid on | Changes the decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PolicyEffect` | `@apf_effect("<name>")` | `permit` only | No. It changes the request and may raise the advisory verdict. An effect that cannot be applied denies the request. |
| `PolicyFinding` | `@apf_finding("<name>")`, or an effect's `finding` field | `permit` and `forbid` | No. It is recorded with the decision. A finding that cannot be resolved denies the request. |

## A First Example

This effect replaces the whole body of a request that carries a secret, tags the request with the kind of secret, and records a finding:

```yaml
apiVersion: nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1
kind: PolicyEffect
metadata:
  name: redact-wholesale
spec:
  description: Replace full body with a redaction notice and emit a secret finding.
  verdict: allow
  reason: secret_pattern_redacted
  body:
    replace: '{"apf_redacted": true, "reason": "credential pattern detected"}'
  headers:
    - name: x-openshell-middleware-apf-event
      action: set
      source: context.annotations.secret_kind
  finding: secret-detected
```

```yaml
apiVersion: nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1
kind: PolicyFinding
metadata:
  name: secret-detected
spec:
  description: Credential material observed in outbound content.
  type: secret_detected
  severity: critical
  label_source: context.annotations.secret_kind
```

A control rule attaches them:

```cedar
@apf_effect("redact-wholesale")
@id("redact-secret-rest")
permit (principal, action, resource)
when { !context.has_tool_name && context.annotations.secret_detected };
```

## PolicyEffect

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `verdict` | `allow`, `warn`, or `escalate`. An advisory signal recorded with the allow. The strongest verdict across all fired effects wins. |
| `reason` | Machine-readable reason for a non-default verdict. |
| `message` | Human-readable message for a non-default verdict. |
| `body.replace` | A string that replaces the whole request body. |
| `body.patches` | A list of RFC 6902 operations: `op` of `replace`, `add`, or `remove`, a JSON Pointer `path`, and a `value` or `source`. |
| `headers` | A list of header mutations: `name`, `action` of `set`, `add`, or `remove`, and a `value` or `source`. |
| `finding` | The name of a `PolicyFinding`, or an inline finding. |

The `body` block is optional, so an effect can change only headers, the verdict, or findings. If you set `body`, set exactly one of `body.replace` and `body.patches`. A `replace` or `add` patch, and a `set` or `add` header, takes exactly one of `value` and `source`. A `remove` takes neither.

### Reading Values from Annotations

`source` copies an annotation's value into a patch or header at evaluation time. It must start with `context.annotations.`, for example `context.annotations.secret_kind`. If the annotation was not produced for the request, the whole evaluation fails closed and the request is denied with the reason `runtime_error:missing_annotation_source:<source>`.

### Header Rules on OpenShell

The OpenShell middleware enforces extra rules on header mutations. A mutation that breaks them denies the request.

- `set` and `add` may only write headers whose names start with `x-openshell-middleware-`.
- `remove` may not remove `authorization`, `proxy-authorization`, `proxy-authenticate`, `cookie`, `host`, `content-length`, `transfer-encoding`, `connection`, `proxy-connection`, `keep-alive`, `te`, `trailer`, or `upgrade`, or any header that starts with `x-amz-` or `x-openshell-credential`.
- Header values must be printable text.

### Patches

Patches apply to the parsed JSON body in firing order. A patch on a request whose body is not JSON, or a `replace` or `remove` on a path the body does not contain, denies the request. `add` creates the target member where RFC 6902 allows it.

```yaml
apiVersion: nvidia.agent-policy-fabric.policy/v1alpha1
kind: PolicyEffect
metadata:
  name: redact-pii-body
spec:
  description: Replace the JSON body's text field on PII detection.
  verdict: allow
  body:
    patches:
      - op: replace
        path: /text
        value: "[APF sanitized: PII detected in message. Original content withheld.]"
  finding:
    type: pii_redacted
    label: pii_in_body_text
    severity: medium
```

### Aggregation

When several permits with effects fire, APF combines them deterministically: patches accumulate in firing order, the last body replacement wins and takes precedence over patches, header mutations accumulate in order, and the strongest verdict wins. The `reason` and `message` come from the first fired effect that carries the final verdict.

## PolicyFinding

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `type` | Finding category, such as `secret_detected`. Recorded as `kind` in audit events. Required. |
| `severity` | `low`, `medium`, `high`, or `critical`. Required. |
| `label` | A static label within the category. |
| `label_source` | An annotation path, such as `context.annotations.secret_kind`, whose value becomes the label. It takes precedence over `label`. |

An inline finding inside an effect has the same fields plus an optional `confidence` from 0 to 100.

A finding with `label_source` fails closed: if the annotation is absent when the finding is resolved, the request is denied, even if `label` is also set. Keep the patterns of a detection flag and its classification label aligned so the label is always produced when the flag is.

## Load-Time Checks

The evaluator refuses to build, and the gateway keeps or refuses the policy, when:

- `@apf_effect` appears on a `forbid`.
- `@apf_effect` or `@apf_finding` names an effect or finding that is not in the bundle.
- An effect's `finding` names a finding that is not in the bundle.
- A `source` or `label_source` does not start with `context.annotations.`.
- An effect sets both or neither of `body.replace` and `body.patches`, or a patch or header has the wrong operands.

Two effects or two findings with the same name are rejected earlier, when the policy service loads the bundle.

## Where Findings Go

Findings travel with the decision to OpenShell and into the `findings` array of the `authorization` audit record. A finding does not change the decision, unless it cannot be resolved, as with a missing `label_source` annotation, or the request exceeds the finding limits. Both deny the request. Refer to [Understand Decisions and Findings](/observability/understand-decisions-and-findings).

## Next Steps

- To check effects and findings before you sign, refer to [Validate and Test Policies](/author-policies/validate-and-test-policies).
- To see effects applied end to end, refer to [Protect Sensitive Data](/tutorials/protect-sensitive-data).

title: "Backup and Recovery"
sidebar-title: "Backup and Recovery"
description: "The state an APF host keeps, what to back up and how, and how to recover from service, host, and policy failures."
keywords: "Generative AI, Cybersecurity, AI Agents, Backup, Recovery, Counter Store, Disaster Recovery, Operations"
position: 6
---

APF keeps little state on a host. Most of what it needs, the signed bundle, trust roots, and keys, comes from your deployment and publish pipelines and can be reinstalled. The anti-rollback counter is the one piece of state that only the host has, and it needs deliberate handling.

## State on a Host

| State | Location on a systemd host | Source of truth | Back up? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Service settings | `/etc/apf/*.env` | Your deployment pipeline. | Rebuild from the pipeline. |
| Signed bundle | `/etc/apf/bundle/` | Your artifact store. | Rebuild from the artifact store. |
| Trust roots | `/etc/apf/trust-roots/` | Your signing authority. | Rebuild from the pipeline. |
| Document signing key, TLS keys, tokens | `/etc/apf/document-signing-key`, `/etc/apf/tls/`, `/etc/apf/http-bearer-token` | Your secret manager. | Reissue or restore from the secret manager. Never copy into ordinary backups. |
| Extension trust profiles | `/etc/apf/openshell-*-auth.toml` | The OpenShell gateway's configuration. | Rebuild from the pipeline. |
| Anti-rollback counter | `/var/lib/apf/policy-service/counter` and `counter.digest` | The host. | Yes. See below. |
| Audit records | The audit directories | Your log pipeline, once shipped. | Ship off the host. |

The policy gateway keeps no policy state of its own. It rebuilds its evaluator from the policy service at startup.

## The Anti-Rollback Counter

The counter records the highest bundle revision the policy service accepted. Losing it, or restoring an older copy, lets the host accept an older signed bundle again.

- **Back it up after each activation**, or at least as often as you publish bundles.
- **Treat counter loss as a security event.** A missing counter reads as `0`, as on a fresh install. Before you restart the service, make sure the only bundle it can load is the current one.
- **Do not restore an older counter** to work around a rejection. Publish a bundle with a higher revision instead.
- **A corrupt counter stops the service.** It refuses to start until an operator restores a good copy or removes the files deliberately.

## Recovery Scenarios

| Situation | What happens | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| The policy service stops while the gateway runs. | The gateway keeps deciding requests with its current evaluator and logs failed polls. New sandbox admissions fail closed because the interceptor cannot fetch the projection. | Restart the policy service. |
| The gateway restarts while the policy service is down. | The gateway cannot fetch the policy set and does not start. With `fail_closed` registrations, OpenShell refuses governed operations. | Start the policy service first, then the gateway. |
| A bad bundle is delivered by refresh or poll. | The policy service keeps the current bundle. A verification failure is recorded. A compilation or fetch failure is only logged. | Fix the bundle and publish a higher revision. Refer to [Update Policies](/manage-policy-bundles/update-policies#recover-from-a-rejected-update). |
| A bad bundle is installed in place and the policy service restarts. | The policy service rejects the bundle and does not start. | Restore the previous bundle files, or install a fixed bundle with a higher revision. |
| The active bundle expires and the policy service restarts. | The policy service rejects the bundle and does not start. | Publish a re-signed bundle with a later `expires_at` and a higher revision. |
| A host is rebuilt. | All local state is gone. | Reinstall from your pipelines, restore the counter from backup, then start the services. |
| A signing key is compromised. | Bundles signed with it are accepted until its trust root is removed. | Sign a replacement bundle with a new key, put it where each policy service loads it at startup, install the new trust root, remove the compromised one, and restart. Refer to [Signing Keys and Trust Roots](/security/signing-keys-and-trust-roots). |

## Backup Tooling

The repository does not include backup or restore tooling. Use your platform's tools, and keep backups of the counter under the same access controls as the counter itself.

- To understand the counter in depth, refer to [Expiry and Rollback Protection](/manage-policy-bundles/expiry-and-rollback-protection).

An `authorization` record is APF's evidence for one decision on one request. It says whether the request was allowed, why, under which policy, what policy observed in it, and what policy changed before it went out.

## An Example

This is the shape of the record the middleware writes when the demo bundle redacts a secret from a plain HTTP request. Values are illustrative.

```json
{
  "schema_version": "apf.audit.event.v1",
  "event_id": "<uuid>",
  "timestamp": "2026-10-07T10:15:02.118Z",
  "event_type": "authorization",
  "correlation_id": "<OpenShell request ID>",
  "enforcement_point_id": "apf-policy-gateway:middleware",
  "runtime_substrate": "openshell",
  "component": {
    "name": "apf-policy-gateway-middleware",
    "version": "0.1.0",
    "instance_id": "apf-policy-gateway:middleware@<host>"
  },
  "session_id": "<sandbox ID>",
  "bundle_digest": "<digest of the policy set the evaluator was built from>",
  "policy_revision": 2,
  "trust_root_id": "apf-policy-service:signing",
  "resource": { "type": "openshell.egress", "id": "httpbin.org" },
  "verb": "http.post",
  "decision": "allow",
  "decision_id": "<id>",
  "reason_code": "middleware.allowed_with_findings",
  "findings": [
    { "kind": "secret_detected", "label": "demo_secret", "severity": "critical" }
  ],
  "effects": {
    "payload_replaced": true,
    "header_mutations": [
      { "name": "x-openshell-middleware-apf-event", "action": "set" }
    ]
  }
}
```

## Decision, Verdict, and Outcome

Three fields describe how something went. They are independent.

| Field | Values | Appears on | Answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| `decision` | `allow`, `deny`. The schema reserves `require_review`, `require_step_up`, `quarantine`, and `stop_session`. | `authorization` only | May this request proceed? |
| `verdict` | `warn`, `escalate` | Middleware `authorization` records, only when an effect raised it | Did policy attach an advisory signal to the allow? Absent means no advisory signal, not "allowed". Records from the gateway's `EvaluationService` always carry a `verdict`, and it reads `allow` on denies, so read `decision` there. |
| `outcome` | `success`, `failure`, `refused` | Every other operation event | How did the operation go? `refused` is a deliberate rejection. `failure` is an operational error. |

## Where the Record Comes From

| Producer | `resource` | `verb` | `reason_code` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Supervisor middleware | `type` `openshell.egress`, `id` the destination host | `tool.<name>` for an MCP tool call, otherwise `http.<method>` | `middleware.allowed`, `middleware.allowed_with_findings`, or `middleware.<deny code>` |
| Gateway `EvaluationService` | `type` the request's `resource.class`, `id` the request's `resource.id` | The request's `verb` | `policy.request_allowed` or `policy.request_denied` |

On a denial, `error.code` repeats the reason code, and `error.message` carries the policy's own reason, such as `security-content-gate/deny-secret` or `no grant for github_repo_write`. A denial by a fail-closed policy information provider carries `pip_<status>:<provider>` there.

When the Enrichment stage ran, the record also carries `extensions.x_apf_pip`, with one entry per provider: its `domain`, which is the registration's `context`, its `provider` name, `status`, whether it `degraded`, `cached`, which is always `false` in this release, its `age_seconds`, its `evidence_ref`, and its `latency_ms`. Refer to [Policy Information Providers](/integrations/policy-information-providers#audit-extension).

Refer to [Supervisor Middleware](/integrations/openshell/supervisor-middleware#deny-reason-codes) for every middleware deny code.

## Findings and Effects

Findings record what policy observed. Effects record what policy did.

| Field | Contents | Present when |
|---|---|---|
| `findings` | Up to 32 entries of `kind`, `label`, `severity`, and optional `confidence`. One entry per firing, not deduplicated, in bundle and policy order. | A fired statement or effect referenced a finding. Omitted when empty. |
| `effects.payload_replaced` | `true` when the body was replaced wholesale. | A body replacement was applied. |
| `effects.patch_count`, `effects.patches` | The number of body patches, and up to 64 patch records with each path and operation. Never the patched value. `patch_count` stays exact when the list is truncated. | Body patches were applied. |
| `effects.header_mutations` | Each mutated header's name and action. Never the value. | Headers were set, added, or removed. |

`effects` is omitted when the request was not changed.

A finding does not change the decision, unless it cannot be resolved or the findings exceed the limits, which denies the request. A redaction record carries both: the finding that a secret was seen, and the effect that the body was replaced. Together they show the request was allowed, flagged, and neutralized.

## Which Policy Decided

Each component names the policy it used by the digest of the document it actually used.

| Component | `bundle_digest` is the digest of |
|---|---|
| Policy service | The signed manifest file for verification and load records. With the HTTP source, hot-swap and distribution records use the downloaded archive instead. |
| Policy gateway and middleware | The `apf.policy.v1` policy set the evaluator was built from. |
| Interceptor | The sandbox policy document injected at admission, or `unverified` when the record was written before anything was verified, as for provider and proposal governance and early refusals. |

To join records across components for the same bundle, use `policy_revision`. Only the policy service records `bundle_id`. The gateway's revision stays at the previous value when a bundle changes no rules, annotators, effects, or findings, and the interceptor's provider and proposal governance records omit the revision.
